name: Mel Brooks
teaser: Brooks was a comedy writer for Sid Caesar's Your Show of Shows before directing — he won an Oscar for his 11-minute short The Critic, then spent years convincing studios to let him make The Producers.

exploreAction.targetName: The Producers (1967), 'Springtime for Hitler'
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the musical number that nearly ended his career before it started. Brooks's joke is that bad taste, performed with total sincerity, becomes art. Notice the precision of the choreography inside the chaos.

name: Woody Allen
teaser: Allen has written, directed, and often starred in a film nearly every year since 1969 — he claims he writes a new script every summer while on holiday.

exploreAction.targetName: Annie Hall (1977), the opening monologue
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Allen breaks the fourth wall in the first minute with a joke about his own childhood. The film's structure — memory, jokes, asides — became the template for the modern rom-com.

name: Sydney Pollack
teaser: Pollack was also a character actor — he played the agent in Tootsie and Dustin Hoffman's boss in Eyes Wide Shut, and directed 20 features between his cameos.

exploreAction.targetName: Tootsie (1982), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Michael Dorsey's agent (Pollack himself) trying to talk sense into him. The film's joke is that Pollack cast himself as the frustrated voice of reason.

name: Robert Zemeckis
teaser: Zemeckis met Steven Spielberg when Spielberg saw his student films at USC — Spielberg then produced the movie that made Zemeckis famous, Back to the Future.

exploreAction.targetName: Back to the Future (1985), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the clocks, the Delorean, the Libyans. Zemeckis sets up the entire trilogy's rules in the first act: time travel, consequences, and a clock that's always running.

name: Robert Aldrich
teaser: Aldrich made The Dirty Dozen and Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? — he was a contract director who outlasted the studio system by being tougher than it.

exploreAction.targetName: Whatever Happened to Baby Jane? (1962), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the child star, the accident, the sisters frozen in time. Aldrich stages the horror of aging inside one house; notice how the house itself becomes a prison.

name: Sam Peckinpah
teaser: Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch made slow-motion violence an art form — the studio thought he'd destroyed the film, and audiences made it a hit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wild Bunch (1969), the opening shootout
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening massacre — children watching a gang's violence as if it were theater. Peckinpah's slow motion makes each death a choice. Notice the children's faces: the film's conscience.

name: William Friedkin
teaser: Friedkin got the directing job on The Exorcist partly because he'd made The French Connection — the studio wanted a realist to shoot the supernatural.

exploreAction.targetName: The Exorcist (1973), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening in Iraq — the archaeology dig, the statue, the wind. Friedkin spends the first act in a completely different world, so the horror arrives slowly. Notice the sound design: the wind is a character.

name: George A. Romero
teaser: Romero invented the modern zombie with Night of the Living Dead — he was a commercial filmmaker who shot the film on weekends with borrowed money and cast his friends.

exploreAction.targetName: Night of the Living Dead (1968), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the cemetery, the first zombie, the farmhouse. Romero made the film for $114,000 and it outgrossed many studio pictures. Notice the grainy black-and-white texture — that's poverty becoming style.

name: John Carpenter
teaser: Carpenter scored his own films on synthesizers — he composed the Halloween theme in one evening because the studio refused to pay for a composer.

exploreAction.targetName: Halloween (1978), the opening POV shot
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a killer's point of view, a young girl, a kitchen knife. Carpenter's opening is a perfect loop: the movie starts and ends with the same idea. Notice the theme's rhythm: 5/4 time, a heartbeat.

name: Tobe Hooper
teaser: Hooper's The Texas Chain Saw Massacre was rated X on release and banned in several countries — it's now in the National Film Registry for its influence on horror.

exploreAction.targetName: The Texas Chain Saw Massacre (1974), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the radio news, the graveyard, the hitchhiker. Hooper shot in the Texas heat with a cast near collapse. Notice how the sun itself feels threatening — horror in daylight.

name: Wes Craven
teaser: Craven based Freddy Krueger's glove on a news story about a man who was attacked by a boiler worker — and Freddy's name came from a bully from Craven's childhood.

exploreAction.targetName: A Nightmare on Elm Street (1984), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Tina's dream, the boiler room, the glove scraping metal. Craven's idea was that the dream IS real. Notice how he breaks the rules of film grammar — the dream logic — to unsettle you.

name: Dario Argento
teaser: Argento's Suspiria is famous for its saturated primary colors — he chose the look after watching Disney's Snow White and deciding horror should be just as colorful.

exploreAction.targetName: Suspiria (1977), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the airport, the taxi, the rain, the ballet school. Argento floods every frame with red, blue, and green gels. Notice how the murders are more like music videos than realistic violence.

name: Stanley Donen
teaser: Donen directed Singin' in the Rain with Gene Kelly — and choreographed most of the dance numbers himself before he was 30.

exploreAction.targetName: Singin' in the Rain (1952), the title number
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the rain dance and notice the tap tempo — Kelly's splashy joy is technically perfect, every step audible in the mix. Donen and Kelly built the number around a single puddle and a lamppost.

name: Vincente Minnelli
teaser: Minnelli directed some of MGM's greatest musicals — including Meet Me in St. Louis, starring his future wife Judy Garland — and his daughter is Liza Minnelli.

exploreAction.targetName: Meet Me in St. Louis (1944), 'Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas'
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Christmas scene — Garland singing a song about separation to her screen sister. Minnelli stages the whole family's grief in one room. The song was written for the film and became a standard.

name: Gene Kelly
teaser: Kelly directed several musicals solo after learning the craft from Donen — he insisted on dancing in real locations, like the rain, because he thought dance belonged in the real world.

exploreAction.targetName: An American in Paris (1951), the final ballet
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 17-minute dream ballet at the end. Kelly designed it as a living painting — every scene references a different French painter. Notice how the choreography becomes the plot's resolution.

name: Bob Fosse
teaser: Fosse directed All That Jazz, a movie about his own heart attack — he survived open-heart surgery in real life and turned it into a musical.

exploreAction.targetName: All That Jazz (1979), the opening 'audition' sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the dancer's audition with the casting table, the heartbeat sound, the mirrors. Fosse's editing is staccato, like jazz. Notice how the film is already a confession.

name: Roger Corman
teaser: Corman produced over 400 films on tiny budgets and gave debuts to Coppola, Scorsese, Bogdanovich, and many more — his movies were shot in days, not weeks.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Shop of Horrors (1960), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the flower shop, the plant, the blood. Corman shot the film in two days by reusing the same sets. Notice how poverty of resources forces inventive camera angles.

name: Russ Meyer
teaser: Meyer's Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! was a drive-in sensation — his films were cheap, fast, and so stylish that even the art world eventually embraced them.

exploreAction.targetName: Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! (1965), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the go-go dancers, the desert, the violence. Meyer shoots with a comic book's energy: wide angles, rapid cuts, and dialogue that's pure pulp poetry.

name: Hal Ashby
teaser: Ashby edited 2001 for Kubrick before directing — his films like Harold and Maude and Being There have a gentle, humane eccentricity that made him a 1970s icon.

exploreAction.targetName: Being There (1979), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Chance the gardener watching television, his whole world. Ashby's joke is that the simple man's platitudes are mistaken for wisdom. Notice how the TV is framed like a window.

name: Terry Gilliam
teaser: Gilliam was the only American in Monty Python — he did the animated sequences — and his solo films like Brazil and 12 Monkeys mix comedy with dystopia.

exploreAction.targetName: Brazil (1985), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the bureaucratic dream world, the giant ducts, the paperwork. Gilliam built a dystopia from office supplies. Notice how the sets look hand-built, like his animations come to life.

name: Jean-Pierre Jeunet
teaser: Jeunet made Amélie after Delicatessen and Alien: Resurrection — the film's saturated Paris became a global postcard, though he shot much of it in a studio with CGI street extensions.

exploreAction.targetName: Amélie (2001), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the childhood, the goldfish, the neighbor. Jeunet's Paris is a cartoon of itself, painted green and red. Notice how every frame is staged like a diorama.

name: Luc Besson
teaser: Besson wrote Léon: The Professional at 20 and says it's the film he'd make forever — he opened a film school, Cité du Cinéma, to teach his own visual style.

exploreAction.targetName: Léon: The Professional (1994), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the hit, the milk, the plant. Besson establishes the hitman's routines before the plot arrives. Notice the milk: a ritual that makes a killer human.

name: Gaspar Noé
teaser: Noé's Irreversible is famous for its backwards narrative and a nine-minute unbroken shot of violence — audiences walked out, and it's still discussed today.

exploreAction.targetName: Irréversible (2002), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening backwards scenes — the film runs in reverse, so you meet the ending first. Noé's camera spins and floats; notice how the chaos is choreographed. This film is an endurance test by design.

name: Franco Zeffirelli
teaser: Zeffirelli directed the 1968 Romeo and Juliet with real teenagers — Leonard Whiting was 16 and Olivia Hussey 15, and their casting changed how the play was performed forever.

exploreAction.targetName: Romeo and Juliet (1968), the balcony scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the balcony scene — Zeffirelli shot it in a real Italian courtyard with real light. His casting of actual adolescents made the romance feel dangerous and new. Notice the costumes: Renaissance, not Elizabethan.

name: Luchino Visconti
teaser: Visconti was a Milanese aristocrat and communist who made The Leopard, a three-hour epic about the Sicilian nobility — he was both the aristocrat and the critic of the aristocrat.

exploreAction.targetName: The Leopard (1963), the ballroom sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final hour's ballroom scene — 20 minutes of waltz that ends the film. Visconti stages the death of an aristocracy in a single dance. Notice the sweat, the champagne, the dying light.

name: Roberto Rossellini
teaser: Rossellini shot Rome Open City during the actual Nazi occupation with smuggled film stock — his actors wore real clothes from the street, and some scenes were shot while the Germans still held the city.

exploreAction.targetName: Rome, Open City (1945), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the resistance cell, the streets, the raids. Rossellini invented neorealism here: real streets, real fear, no studio. Notice how the documentary grain IS the authenticity.
